question.prompt: Let \(f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}\) be defined by \(f(z) = z^2 + iz + 1.\) How many complex numbers \(z\) are there such that \(\operatorname{Im}(z) \gt 0\) and both the real and the imaginary parts of \(f(z)\) are integers with absolute value at most \(10?\)

solutions.explanation:
Write \(z=x+iy\), where \(x,y\) are real and \(y>0\). Expanding gives
\[
f(z)=(x^2-y^2-y+1)+i\,x(2y+1).
\]
Suppose \(f(z)=a+bi\), where \(a,b\) are integers between \(-10\) and \(10\). Comparing imaginary parts gives \(x=b/(2y+1)\). This denominator is positive because \(y>0\).

The factor \(2y+1\) suggests setting \(t=(2y+1)^2>1\). Then \(x^2=b^2/t\) and \(y^2+y=(t-1)/4\), so the real-part equation becomes
\[
a=\frac{b^2}{t}+\frac{5-t}{4}.
\]
Since \(t>1\), multiplication by \(4t\) is valid and yields
\[
Q(t)=t^2+(4a-5)t-4b^2=0.
\]
Conversely, any root \(t>1\) gives exactly one eligible complex number through
\[
y=\frac{\sqrt t-1}{2},\qquad x=\frac{b}{\sqrt t}.
\]
These formulas satisfy both original component equations, so it remains to count roots greater than \(1\).

If \(b\ne0\), the discriminant of \(Q\) is positive and its root product is \(-4b^2<0\). Thus it has one negative root and one positive root. Since \(1\) lies to the right of the negative root, the positive root exceeds \(1\) exactly when
\[
Q(1)=4(a-1-b^2)<0.
\]
For integer \(a\), this is equivalent to \(a\le b^2\). Equality \(Q(1)=0\) gives \(y=0\), which is excluded.

If \(b=0\), the equation factors as \(t(t+4a-5)=0\). Its only possible root greater than \(1\) is \(t=5-4a\), which works exactly when \(a<1\), or \(a\le0=b^2\). Therefore, in every case, an integer output has exactly one eligible preimage if \(a\le b^2\), and none otherwise.

There are \(21^2=441\) candidate integer outputs. Count the excluded ones with \(a>b^2\): for \(b=0\), there are \(10\); for each of \(b=\pm1\), there are \(9\); for each of \(b=\pm2\), there are \(6\); and for each of \(b=\pm3\), there is \(1\). When \(|b|\ge4\), no output is excluded because \(b^2\ge16>10\). Thus the excluded count is
\[
10+2(9+6+1)=42.
\]
The correspondence proved above counts every eligible \(z\) once, so the answer is \(441-42=\boxed{399}\), choice \(\text{A}\).
solutions.title: Determine which integer outputs have one eligible preimage
